paras: The lynching of William Fambro was the killing of Will (William) Fambro, a Black man, by a party of about fifteen white men who fired into his home near Griffin, Spalding County, Georgia, early on February 24, 1903. Fambro had already pleaded guilty and been fined for an offense committed weeks earlier, described as insulting a white woman and her child or as an indecent exposure while drunk. The Governor offered rewards for the killers, and Georgia papers and Black weeklies alike called the killing unjustified.

Fambro lived on the place of H. F. Thurman, half a mile beyond the Spalding Mills outside Griffin. According to a Griffin dispatch to the Savannah Morning News, in early January he "while drunk made an indecent exposure," pleaded guilty in Superior Court, and was fined $40, which Thurman paid and Fambro was working off.

At about 2 a.m. some fifteen men came out of the woods near the house and opened fire with shotguns and Winchester rifles, "shooting hundreds of holes in the building." When Fambro's wife refused them admittance at the front door, they broke out a panel and fired several guns through the opening. One of the first shots struck Fambro in the right breast, and he staggered into the adjoining kitchen and fell dead.

Unaware that he was dead, the men ordered his wife to bring him out and threatened to burn the house if she refused. Thurman came near but was unarmed, and the men withdrew to the woods, still firing, only after the woman was told that help was coming. His wife escaped injury; the Birmingham Age-Herald said three children were also in the house.

The Griffin correspondent called the killing "greatly regretted" and said an effort would be made to find the guilty. On February 26 Governor Terrell offered $250 for the arrest, with proof to convict, of each of the killers, as he did in a Coffee County case in which white men fired into a Black dance. No report of arrests, an inquest, a grand jury inquiry or a trial appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press dispatch ran on February 25 in papers including the Indianapolis Journal, the New-York Tribune and the News & Observer. The Indianapolis Journal grouped it with a Louisiana case under "Two Negroes Lynched," the Omaha Daily Bee said the "Georgia Mob Wreaks Vengeance on Negro Who Insulted White Woman," and the New-York Tribune used the ironic heading "The Best Friend of the Negro." Weekly news digests cut the story to a line saying Fambro had insulted a white woman.

In Georgia the Savannah Morning News ran the fullest account under the headline "Paid With His Life" and called the killing "one of the most unwarranted in the annals of Spalding county." Its editorial of February 26, "Time to Call a Halt," called the killing "cruel and cold-blooded" and asked what the Spalding County grand jury would do, while holding that public sentiment "seems to justify lynch law" when the victim had assaulted a woman. The Birmingham Age-Herald named Georgia "the lynching state of the union" but dismissed the Governor's rewards as "simply grandstand plays."

On February 28 the Richmond Planet reprinted the wire dispatch in an editorial answering Senator B. R. Tillman, as one of two lynchings in the same telegraph reports that were not for "criminal assaults." The Savannah Tribune wrote that a colored man "was murdered by a mob at Griffin" for an old offense and that "these murderers should be brought to justice," and the Colored American noted that "Georgia white people lynched a Negro at Griffin." Midyear lynching lists from The Striker, reprinted in three Black weeklies, entered Fambro under February 24, one giving his offense as "insulting whites."

Accounts of the earlier offense differ: the AP said Fambro had been charged with "insulting a white woman and her child," the Griffin correspondent described an indecent exposure while drunk, and an Atlanta report said he "insulted a lady and child while intoxicated." Only the AP mentions a chain-gang sentence, and the Savannah Tribune said he was "serving time" for an offense "several months ago," whereas the local report dates it to early January.

reader.title: Lynching of William Fambro
bases: A party of about fifteen white men fired into Fambro's home at night and killed him for an offense for which he had already been fined (A5, A14); white and Black papers called it a lynching (A2, A11, A28).

Fambro was shot dead in his home by 'a party of about 15 men' acting without any legal authority (A5, A14), and the papers tied the killing to punishing his earlier offense, the Savannah Morning News headline saying white men 'decided to visit extreme penalty' after the court had fined him (A5, A11).
The AP dispatch (A2, A3) and the separate Griffin correspondent's report in the Savannah Morning News (A5) agree on the core event, and the Governor's reward notice from Atlanta confirms it (A14).

accounts.label: Wire report (AP, Griffin)
accounts.gist: A mob fired more than a thousand shots into Fambro's house late Monday night and killed him; he had been arrested for insulting a white woman and her child, sentenced to the chain gang, and his fine paid by his employer.

accounts.label: Griffin correspondent, Savannah Morning News
accounts.gist: About fifteen white men attacked at 2 a.m., fired through a broken door panel, killed Fambro and threatened to burn the house; his offense had been an indecent exposure while drunk, for which he pleaded guilty and was fined $40.

accounts.label: Governor's reward notice (Atlanta)
accounts.gist: An angry mob of white men fired into Fambro's home on the night of Feb. 23 after he had been fined for insulting a lady and child while intoxicated; the Governor offered $250 per murderer.

accounts.label: Black editorial comment
accounts.gist: A colored man was murdered by a mob for an old offense he was already being punished for; the case disproved the claim that lynchings answer criminal assault.
